nameStory: The name 'devil's-claw' comes from the plant's distinctive seed pods that split into two curved, claw-like hooks that look downright menacing. These fearsome-looking 'claws' can grab onto fur, clothing, or anything that brushes past, earning this plant its devilish reputation. The alternative name 'unicorn plant' refers to the long, curved horn-like projection on the young seed pods.
description: Common devil's-claw is an unusual annual plant that looks more like it belongs in a desert than in New England. It grows as a sprawling, somewhat sticky plant with large heart-shaped leaves and showy purple or pink flowers that bloom in summer. The real showstopper is the bizarre seed pod that starts as a long curved 'horn' and eventually splits into two wicked-looking claws. This southwestern native occasionally shows up as an escape from gardens where it's grown as a curiosity.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The unmistakable seed pods are this plant's calling card - they start as long curved horns up to 6 inches long, then split into two fierce-looking claws with sharp hooks. The pods feel woody and tough when mature.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Trumpet-shaped flowers are purple, pink, or sometimes white with darker spots inside. They're about 1-2 inches long and have an irregular, orchid-like shape that's quite showy.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, heart-shaped leaves feel somewhat sticky and clammy to the touch due to tiny hairs. They're arranged alternately on the stem and can be 6-12 inches across.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a sprawling, somewhat weedy-looking annual plant that can spread 2-3 feet wide. The whole plant has a slightly sticky, hairy texture and a distinctive musky smell.

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region. When found, it's typically as an escape from cultivation in disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, or near old garden sites. This southwestern native prefers warm, sunny locations with well-drained soil.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring after soils warm up. Young plants develop their characteristic large, sticky heart-shaped leaves.
seasonality.summer: Showy purple flowers bloom from mid to late summer, followed by the development of the distinctive curved horn-like seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split into their famous two-pronged claws. The plant dies with first frost, but the woody seed pods persist.
seasonality.winter: Only the distinctive woody seed pods remain, often still clinging to dead plant material or scattered on the ground.

funFact: This plant is sometimes called the 'aphid trap' because its sticky leaves and stems naturally catch aphids and other small insects, making it a living pest control system in gardens - though the plant itself isn't carnivorous and doesn't digest the bugs!
confusionNotes: The large heart-shaped leaves might remind you of morning glory or wild cucumber, but the sticky texture and musky smell are distinctive. Once you see the bizarre curved seed pods, there's absolutely nothing else it could be - they're completely unique in New England.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'Louisiana unicorn-plant,' this species isn't actually native to Louisiana - its true native range is the Southwest. The 'Louisiana' part of the scientific name (louisianica) is a historical naming confusion that stuck. It's grown as a novelty plant for its weird seed pods, which are popular in dried flower arrangements.
compareHints: Common devil's-claw is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique in the region. Within its family (Martyniaceae), it's distinguished from other devil's claw species by being the most widely distributed and having purple flowers rather than yellow or white ones. No other plant family in New England produces anything remotely like its distinctive clawed seed pods.
